introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »). Aucun écart constaté : les questions à plusieurs parties somment bien 25 (Q4 : 9 + 8 + 8 ; Q31 : 12 + 13 ; Q36 : 5 + 20). Les points imprimés n'ont pas été modifiés.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde puis 36 questions en six sections de six) : filigrane gcerevision.com et texte fantôme du verso ignorés ; aucune question illisible, aucune figure ni carte. Les doubles espaces imprimés ont été normalisés.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level, avec des références bibliques ou islamiques limitées à celles que l'auteur tient pour sûres ; formulations prudentes (« according to Islamic tradition », « Christians believe »). À faire relire par un spécialiste (théologie chrétienne, histoire de l'islam, philosophie de la religion) avant mise en avant.

Question 5 : la phrase imprimée (« ... communicating a common idea about the Kingdom, they contain some basic ideas in common ») est syntaxiquement peu claire ; elle est recopiée telle quelle et le corrigé la lit comme une demande des idées communes aux paraboles sur le Royaume.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Though the parables seem to have been communicating a common idea about the Kingdom, they contain some basic ideas in common. Discuss these basic ideas.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A parable is a short story from daily life used by Jesus to teach about the kingdom (reign) of God. Although each parable has its own point, the parables in Luke share several basic ideas. The sentence in the question is printed in a way that is not perfectly clear; it is understood here as asking for the basic ideas that the parables have in common about the Kingdom.

**1. The Kingdom is God's gift and God's initiative.** The Kingdom is not produced by human effort. The great banquet (Luke 14:15-24) shows God who prepares and sends out the invitation; the father in the story of the prodigal son runs to welcome his son (Luke 15:20). The lost sheep and the lost coin show God as the seeker (Luke 15:3-10).

**2. The Kingdom is present and still to come.** Jesus declares that the Kingdom is "in the midst of you" (Luke 17:20-21), and yet many parables look to a future judgement and reward: the faithful servants who await their master (Luke 12:35-48) and the parable of the pounds, where the nobleman returns as king (Luke 19:11-27). The Kingdom has begun but is not yet complete.

**3. Small beginnings and great results.** The mustard seed and the leaven (Luke 13:18-21) teach that something small and hidden will grow into something great and will transform everything.

**4. The Kingdom is open to all, especially to the lowly and to outcasts.** The poor, the crippled and the blind are brought to the banquet (Luke 14:21); the tax collector is justified rather than the Pharisee (Luke 18:9-14); the Samaritan proves a neighbour (Luke 10:25-37); the lost son is welcomed home. The values of the world are reversed: the rich man who ignores Lazarus is condemned (Luke 16:19-31).

**5. The Kingdom demands a response now.** Repentance, readiness, watchfulness and faithful use of what is entrusted are required. The rich fool loses everything because he did not prepare for God (Luke 12:16-21), and the guests who make excuses lose their place at the feast (Luke 14:18-20).

**6. Joy and celebration.** The Kingdom is presented as a feast. The shepherd, the woman and the father all call their friends to rejoice (Luke 15:6, 9, 23-24).

**7. Judgement.** Those who refuse or neglect the invitation are excluded (Luke 13:25-28; 14:24).

**Conclusion.** Behind the variety of images are common convictions: the Kingdom is God's gift, it has come in Jesus and will be completed, it grows from small beginnings, it welcomes the outcast, and it demands a decisive response. These shared ideas show that the parables are different windows on one proclamation.
